Starting in Python 3.11, the interpreter observes each bytecode instruction as it runs, and after it's been executed a few times with the same operand types, it **quietly rewrites that specific instruction** in memory to a specialized, faster variant tailored to those observed types — skipping the generic type-dispatch logic entirely on subsequent runs, as long as the types keep matching.

This pays off because a generic instruction is expensive. `BINARY_ADD` has to handle every possible combination of operand types — two ints, two floats, a string and an int (error), two custom objects with `__add__` — and it re-checks all of them on every single execution. In real code, a given call site (one specific line of bytecode) usually sees the **same types over and over again**.
